topic: New build inspections: the three walks that are not yours
hook: New builds get inspected three times. None of them for you.

scores.worst_problem: The payoff is scoped only to the pre-drywall walk while the deck's sharpest, most novel beat is the month-eleven warranty deadline, so the artefact under-delivers on half the promise the carousel built.
scores.fix: Widen the DM payoff to cover both windows explicitly — e.g. 'the two-page checklist I hand buyers: what to photograph at pre-drywall and what to flag at month eleven'.

deck.topic: New build inspections: the three walks that are not yours
deck.hook: New builds get inspected three times. None of them for you.

points.title: Who Those Three Serve
body: The city inspector checks code minimums and leaves.
The builder's own walk protects the builder.
The final walkthrough is a paint and scratch tour.

points.title: The Pre-Drywall Window
body: Framing, wiring, plumbing and ducts are visible for about a week.
After insulation and drywall, all of it disappears behind a wall.
Ask for that date the moment the frame goes up.

points.title: The Sign Off Trap
body: At the walkthrough they hand you a punch list and a pen.
Buyers write down nail pops and miss the grading and the attic.
Anything you sign off on quietly becomes yours.

points.title: Month Eleven
body: Most builder workmanship coverage runs one year from closing.
Book your own inspection at month eleven, not month thirteen.
That gives you weeks to file while the claim still counts.

points.title: What It Runs You
body: A pre-drywall visit and an eleven month visit each cost a few hundred.
One missed framing or drainage issue costs many times that.
The builder is never going to offer to book it for you.
points.loop: Knowing what to flag is harder.

linkedinCaption:
Three people walk a new build before you own it. None of them work for you. The city inspector confirms code minimums. The builder's walk protects the builder. The final walkthrough is largely a paint and scratch tour.

That leaves two windows worth paying for. Pre-drywall, when framing, wiring, plumbing and ducts are still visible for roughly a week. And month eleven, before most builder workmanship coverage expires at one year.

Each visit runs a few hundred dollars. A missed framing or drainage issue runs many times that. And the punch list at walkthrough matters more than buyers realize. What you sign off on quietly becomes yours.

For agents working new construction: how early do you raise the pre-drywall inspection with your buyers?
